# Built-in Types

Types every program can name without an import: Odin's basic types, and the three Vidar adds.

## Vidar types

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`Clone`](#clone) | `impl Clone for T { clone = t_clone }`, with `t_clone :: proc(x: T) -> T`, turns every copy of a `T` (which needs `impl Destroy`) into a call to `t_clone`, so each copy has its own owner, as with a C++ copy constructor. |
| [`Destroy`](#destroy) | `impl Destroy for T { destroy = t_destroy }`, with `t_destroy :: proc(x: ^T)`, destroys each local of type `T` when its scope ends, the old value on assignment, and never a local that is returned (it moves out). |
| [`Pool`](#pool) | `Pool(I)` holds values of every implementation of interface `I`, one array per type. |

### `Clone`

`impl Clone for T { clone = t_clone }`, with `t_clone :: proc(x: T) -> T`, turns every copy of a `T` (which needs `impl Destroy`) into a call to `t_clone`, so each copy has its own owner, as with a C++ copy constructor. Structs whose destroyed fields can all be cloned are cloned field by field. The last use of a local moves it instead of cloning. `vidar:rc`'s `Rc(T)` is built on it. Built in unless the program declares its own `Clone`.

See [Copying with `impl Clone`](ch07-03-impl-clone.md).

```vidar
Handle :: struct { id: int, refs: ^int }

handle_destroy :: proc(h: ^Handle) {
	if h.refs == nil do return
	h.refs^ -= 1
	if h.refs^ == 0 {
		fmt.println("last handle to", h.id, "released")
		free(h.refs)
	}
}

handle_clone :: proc(h: Handle) -> Handle {
	h.refs^ += 1
	return h
}

impl Destroy for Handle { destroy = handle_destroy }
impl Clone for Handle { clone = handle_clone }

main :: proc() {
	a := Handle{7, new_clone(1)}
	b := a                 // a clone: a is used below
	fmt.println("refs:", a.refs^, "ids:", a.id, b.id)
}
```

```output
refs: 2 ids: 7 7
last handle to 7 released
```

### `Destroy`

`impl Destroy for T { destroy = t_destroy }`, with `t_destroy :: proc(x: ^T)`, destroys each local of type `T` when its scope ends, the old value on assignment, and never a local that is returned (it moves out). Structs, arrays, unions and `Maybe`s holding a `T` are destroyed too, and so are generic code's values (found at run time). Dynamic arrays and maps own their elements: destroyed with them, and by `clear`, `pop`, `delete_key` and the like; slices are views. `impl Destroy for Box($T)` covers every instance. Copies are compile errors unless `T` has `impl Clone`; borrow with `&x`, or move with `move!(x)`. Built in unless the program declares its own `Destroy`.

The whole of [Chapter 7](ch07-00-destructors.md) is about it.

```vidar
Buffer :: struct { data: []byte }

buffer_destroy :: proc(b: ^Buffer) {
	fmt.println("freeing", len(b.data), "bytes")
	delete(b.data)
}

impl Destroy for Buffer { destroy = buffer_destroy }

main :: proc() {
	b := Buffer{make([]byte, 16)}
	fmt.println("using", len(b.data), "bytes")
}   // b is destroyed here
```

```output
using 16 bytes
freeing 16 bytes
```

### `Pool`

`Pool(I)` holds values of every implementation of interface `I`, one array per type. `for s in pool` loops over each type in turn with `s: ^T`, so method calls are direct. Supports `append` (values), `len`, `clear` and `delete`.

See [Closures, Interfaces and `Pool`](ch15-06-closures-and-interfaces.md#pooli).

```vidar
Shape :: interface { area }
area :: proc(s: Shape) -> f64 ---

Square :: struct { side: f64 }
Circle :: struct { r: f64 }

square_area :: proc(s: ^Square) -> f64 { return s.side * s.side }
circle_area :: proc(c: ^Circle) -> f64 { return 3 * c.r * c.r }

impl Shape for Square { area = square_area }
impl Shape for Circle { area = circle_area }

main :: proc() {
	shapes: Pool(Shape)
	defer delete(shapes)
	append(&shapes, Square{2}, Circle{1}, Square{1})
	total := 0.0
	for s in shapes do total += area(s)     // one loop per type, direct calls
	fmt.println(len(shapes), total)
}
```

```output
3 8
```

## Odin types

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`any`](#any) | Any value, as a pointer to its data and its `typeid`. |
| [`b16`](#b16) | 16-bit boolean. |
| [`b32`](#b32) | 32-bit boolean. |
| [`b64`](#b64) | 64-bit boolean. |
| [`b8`](#b8) | 8-bit boolean. |
| [`bool`](#bool) | Boolean (1 byte). |
| [`byte`](#byte) | Alias of `u8`. |
| [`complex128`](#complex128) | Complex number of two `f64`. |
| [`complex64`](#complex64) | Complex number of two `f32`. |
| [`cstring`](#cstring) | Null-terminated C string. |
| [`f16`](#f16) | 16-bit float. |
| [`f32`](#f32) | 32-bit float. |
| [`f64`](#f64) | 64-bit float. |
| [`i128`](#i128) | 128-bit signed integer. |
| [`i16`](#i16) | 16-bit signed integer. |
| [`i32`](#i32) | 32-bit signed integer. |
| [`i64`](#i64) | 64-bit signed integer. |
| [`i8`](#i8) | 8-bit signed integer. |
| [`int`](#int) | Signed integer of pointer size (64-bit on 64-bit targets). |
| [`quaternion256`](#quaternion256) | Quaternion of four `f64`. |
| [`rawptr`](#rawptr) | Untyped pointer (`void*`). |
| [`rune`](#rune) | A Unicode code point (32-bit). |
| [`string`](#string) | UTF-8 string: a pointer and a byte length. |
| [`u128`](#u128) | 128-bit unsigned integer. |
| [`u16`](#u16) | 16-bit unsigned integer. |
| [`u32`](#u32) | 32-bit unsigned integer. |
| [`u64`](#u64) | 64-bit unsigned integer. |
| [`u8`](#u8) | 8-bit unsigned integer. |
| [`uint`](#uint) | Unsigned integer of pointer size. |
| [`uintptr`](#uintptr) | Unsigned integer large enough to hold a pointer. |

### `any`

Any value, as a pointer to its data and its `typeid`.

```vidar
describe :: proc(x: any) {
	switch v in x {
	case int:    fmt.println("an int:", v)
	case string: fmt.println("a string:", v)
	case:        fmt.println("something else:", x.id)
	}
}

main :: proc() {
	describe(42)
	describe("hi")
	describe(1.5)
}
```

```output
an int: 42
a string: hi
something else: f64
```

### `b16`

16-bit boolean.

```vidar
x: b16 = true
fmt.println(x, size_of(b16))
```

```output
true 2
```

### `b32`

32-bit boolean.

```vidar
x: b32 = 3 > 2
fmt.println(x, size_of(b32))
```

```output
true 4
```

The sized booleans exist for C interop, where a `BOOL` is often 4 bytes.

### `b64`

64-bit boolean.

```vidar
x: b64 = false
fmt.println(x, size_of(b64))
```

```output
false 8
```

### `b8`

8-bit boolean.

```vidar
flags: [4]b8 = {true, false, true, true}
fmt.println(flags, size_of(b8))
```

```output
[true, false, true, true] 1
```

### `bool`

Boolean (1 byte).

```vidar
ready := 2 + 2 == 4
fmt.println(ready, !ready, size_of(bool))
```

```output
true false 1
```

### `byte`

Alias of `u8`.

```vidar
data := []byte{72, 105}
fmt.println(string(data), typeid_of(byte) == typeid_of(u8))
```

```output
Hi true
```

### `complex128`

Complex number of two `f64`.

```vidar
z := complex(0.0, 1.0)     // complex128
fmt.println(z * z, abs(complex(3.0, 4.0)))
```

```output
-1+0i 5
```

### `complex64`

Complex number of two `f32`.

```vidar
z: complex64 = complex(1, 2)
fmt.println(z * z)
```

```output
-3+4i
```

### `cstring`

Null-terminated C string.

```vidar
name: cstring = "vidar"           // a constant string converts to cstring
fmt.println(len(name), string(name))
```

```output
5 vidar
```

Use it for C APIs; `strings.clone_to_cstring` makes one from a run-time `string`.

### `f16`

16-bit float.

```vidar
h: f16 = 1.5
fmt.println(h * 2, size_of(f16))
```

```output
3 2
```

### `f32`

32-bit float.

```vidar
x: f32 = 0.1
fmt.println(x * 3, size_of(f32))
```

```output
0.3 4
```

### `f64`

64-bit float.

```vidar
x := 0.1                 // untyped floats default to f64
fmt.println(x * 3, typeid_of(type_of(x)))
```

```output
0.30000000000000004 f64
```

### `i128`

128-bit signed integer.

```vidar
x: i128 = 1 << 100
fmt.println(x)
```

```output
1267650600228229401496703205376
```

### `i16`

16-bit signed integer.

```vidar
x: i16 = -300
fmt.println(x, size_of(i16))
```

```output
-300 2
```

### `i32`

32-bit signed integer.

```vidar
x: i32 = 2_000_000_000
fmt.println(x, size_of(i32))
```

```output
2000000000 4
```

### `i64`

64-bit signed integer.

```vidar
x: i64 = 1 << 40
fmt.println(x, size_of(i64))
```

```output
1099511627776 8
```

### `i8`

8-bit signed integer.

```vidar
x: i8 = 127
x += 1                   // wraps around
fmt.println(x, min(i8), max(i8))
```

```output
-128 -128 127
```

### `int`

Signed integer of pointer size (64-bit on 64-bit targets).

```vidar
n := 42                  // untyped integers default to int
fmt.println(n, size_of(int), typeid_of(type_of(n)))
```

```output
42 8 int
```

### `quaternion256`

Quaternion of four `f64`.

```vidar
q: quaternion256 = 1
i := quaternion(w = 0, x = 1, y = 0, z = 0)
fmt.println(q, i * i)
```

```output
1+0i+0j+0k -1+0i+0j+0k
```

### `rawptr`

Untyped pointer (`void*`).

```vidar
x := 7
p: rawptr = &x
back := (^int)(p)
fmt.println(back^)
```

```output
7
```

### `rune`

A Unicode code point (32-bit).

```vidar
for r in "héllo" do fmt.print(r, "")
fmt.println()
fmt.println('é', u32('é'))
```

```output
h é l l o
é 233
```

Looping over a string gives its runes, decoded from UTF-8.

### `string`

UTF-8 string: a pointer and a byte length. Not null-terminated.

```vidar
s := "héllo"
fmt.println(len(s), s[1:3], strings.to_upper(s, context.temp_allocator))
```

```output
6 é HÉLLO
```

128-bit unsigned integer.

```vidar
x: u128 = 1 << 127
fmt.println(x)
```

```output
170141183460469231731687303715884105728
```


### `u8`

8-bit unsigned integer.

```vidar
x: u8 = 255

```


### `uint`

Unsigned integer of pointer size.

```vidar
x: uint = 3
fmt.println(x, size_of(uint) == size_of(int))
```

```output
3 true
```

### `uintptr`

Unsigned integer large enough to hold a pointer.

```vidar
x := 7
addr := uintptr(&x)
fmt.println(addr != 0, size_of(uintptr) == size_of(rawptr))
```

```output
true true
```
